title: Kizen Strength & Aesthetics Powerbuilding program review
summary: NH reviews the first four weeks of the Kizen powerbuilding program. He criticizes splitting days into isolation-only superset days and compound-only days with unrelated lifts, unsynergistic supersets, static low-effort rep schemes, wasted low-intensity introductory weeks, junk-volume percentages and no intensity application on isolation work. It may serve only as a bridge for lifters who never isolated.
claims: Programs with constant exercise rotation over 16 weeks are rarely well thought out; four weeks is enough to judge
Everyone is a powerbuilder to some extent, but you cannot be top level at both; top powerlifters are massive but not aesthetic
Six sessions a week is good high frequency, and should come with less volume per session
A day with zero strength work is bad: strength work should open every session, with only occasional exceptions
You cannot separate strength and size into different days; each session needs both
A day of only isolation exercises wastes recovery ability
Superset a vertical press with a vertical pull: specific and synergistic
Supersets of unrelated muscles like cable rows with triceps pushdowns and laterals lack synergy; supersets are not where you perform
French press with hammer curls pairs long-head triceps and biceps well
A whole day of only supersets is a waste of time
Squat, bench and stiff-leg deadlift in one day needs a new warm-up for each and lets the lower body go cold
Bodybuilders already know the main lifts, so starting a program at low intensity wastes tonnage
Two sets at a fixed 12 or 8 reps sandbags the first set; use rep ranges
Small muscles should be trained frequently with less volume
3x5 is one of the best static rep schemes, especially on bench
Incline bench and overhead press in the same day are somewhat redundant; overhead press is my pick
Lifters who never isolated will grow from any isolation work, even poorly programmed; that is why such programs seem to work
Squats, pause squats, bench, deadlift, hamstring curls and planks in one day is too much; a heavy lower-back-loading lift followed by a floor pull is how you get injured
Program low intensity only for new variations, not for lifts the trainee already knows
Fix by redistributing: put bench on the upper isolation day and deadlifts on the upper back day
Two deadlift variations in one day makes no sense; stick to one and progress it
Higher-rep work needs evolving rep ranges across sets, e.g. 6-8 rather than a fixed 8 or a too-wide 5-8
If you can do 15 bodyweight chin-ups, most people should progress to weighted pull-ups as strength work
Squats plus pause squats already cook the hamstrings; no need for extra hamstring curls that day
Planks are redundant with compound bracing; train abs in a stretched position with leg raises
The best ab hypertrophy exercise is crunches on an incline bench
Bodybuilding does not need deloads; deloads are built into session volume and intensity
Match training stress to recovery ability; weeks at low intensity waste recovery because there is nothing to recover from
Matching percentages across same-pattern lifts in a session mismanages intensity because relative intensity rises with fatigue
A movement that cannot be done in a relevant intensity window means the muscle is fatigued; it is junk volume, time to go home
Apply intensity windows to isolation movements too; not progressing on them is why many lifters' arms never grow
I do not recommend Kizen for getting bigger; at most a bridge for those who never isolated
exercises: long head triceps and biceps synergy
